title: WA shines at 2026 Australian Small Winemakers Show
summary:
The 2026 Australian Small Winemakers Show culminated last Friday 23 October with the announcement of trophy winners at Varias restaurant. 2026 is the 40th year of the Australian Small Winemakers Show celebrating the quality, diversity and innovation of Australia’s small-scale wine producers. Wines were received from all wine producing states “showcasing the wide range of varieties and styles produced by small-scale winemakers across Australia”. Organisers shared that Western Australian wineries shone, securing three of the major trophies in the show and 59% overall of all gold medals awarded. Mandoon Estate won the ‘Champion Winery of Show’, ‘Champion Sparkling’ and the ‘Preben Jacobsen Memorial Stewards’ Choice’, with Hamelin Bay Wines winning the ‘Champion White Wine’, and Jadran Wines the ‘Dick De Luca Memorial trophy’ for ‘Champion Shiraz’.

content:
Ray Costanzo, Golden Grove Estate, QLD; Stefan Dewey, Dewey Station Wines, SA; Andrew Sutherland Smith, Warrabilla Wines, VIC. Image supplied

The 2026 Australian Small Winemakers Show culminated last Friday 23 October with the announcement of trophy winners at Varias restaurant in Stanthorpe on Queensland’s Granite Belt.

2026 is the 40th year of the Australian Small Winemakers Show celebrating the quality, diversity and innovation of Australia’s small-scale wine producers. Wines were received from all wine producing states “showcasing the wide range of varieties and styles produced by small-scale winemakers across Australia”.

Organisers shared that Western Australian wineries shone, securing three of the major trophies in the show and 59% overall of all gold medals awarded.

Mandoon Estate won the ‘Champion Winery of Show’, ‘Champion Sparkling’ and the ‘Preben Jacobsen Memorial Stewards’ Choice’, with Hamelin Bay Wines winning the ‘Champion White Wine’, and Jadran Wines the ‘Dick De Luca Memorial trophy’ for ‘Champion Shiraz’.

Dewey Station Wines (SA) won the ‘Champion Rosé’ and Warrabilla Wines (VIC) the ‘Champion Red Wine’, rounding out the major trophies.

Chair of judges Jeremy Dineen noted the diversity of varieties contesting the ‘Champion White Wine of Show’, a Vermentino, Albariño, Semillon, Pecorino and Chardonnay, “reflecting the propensity for small-scale producers to often be leading the way with new alternate varieties”.

Similarly, the ‘Champion Red Wine of Show’ was between a Victorian Durif, Margaret River Malbec, South Australian Sangiovese, Tasmanian Pinot Noir and a Queensland Shiraz/Durif.

Dineen said each wine delivered its own style of drinking pleasure and acknowledged the “very strong class of 2024 Cabernet Sauvignon, with 80% of wines achieving a medal”.

The 2026 Australian Small Winemakers Show concluded with a public tasting on Saturday afternoon attended by nearly 350 wine lovers.

The full list of trophy winners is as follows:

  • Champion Winery of Show, Mandoon Estate (WA)
  • Champion Red Wine, Warrabilla Wines (Vic), 2025 Parola’s Durif
  • Champion White Wine, Hamelin Bay Wines (WA), 2025 Reserve Chardonnay
  • Champion Sparkling, Mandoon Estate (WA), 2018 Reserve Sparkling
  • Champion Rose, Dewey Station Wines (SA), 2026 Moonglow Rose Grenache
  • Best Queensland White Wine, Golden Grove Estate, 2022 Semillon. Presented by Varias
  • Best Queensland Red Wine, Golden Grove Estate, 2025 Shiraz/Durif. Presented by Southern Downs Regional Council
  • Best NSW White Wine, Saddler’s Creek Wines, 2026 Single Suitcase Pecorino
  • Best Victorian White Wine, Ros Ritchie Wines, 2025 Sandy Creek Vineyard Vermentino
  • Best Victorian Red Wine, Warrabilla Wines, 2025 Parola’s Durif
  • Best South Australian White Wine, Dewey Station Wines, 2026 Harmonic Constants Albariño. Presented by Cospak.
  • Best South Australian Red Wine, Berrigan Wines, 2025 Shining Rock Vineyard Sangiovese. Presented by National Storage-Wine Ark
  • Best Western Australian White Wine, Hamelin Bay Wines, 2025 Reserve Chardonnay
  • Best Western Australian Red Wine, Hamelin Bay Wines, 2025 Reserve Malbec
  • Best Tasmanian Red Wine, Bream Creek Vineyard, 2025 Pinot Noir

title: Program for healthier, more resilient vineyards to visit Victorian wine regions this November
summary:
Winegrowers across the Surf Coast, Moorabool Valley and Bellarine Peninsula will soon have access to a nationally recognised program designed to build healthier, more resilient vineyards. Following the success of an introductory event held in the Geelong wine region in May 2026, the EcoVineyards program will be formally launching in the region next month. The program will be open to all winegrowers “interested in improving fruit quality, while building healthier, more productive and resilient vineyards through practical, locally relevant approaches”. The first event is a field day at Barwon Ridge, Barrabool, on Friday 30 November.

The post Program for healthier, more resilient vineyards to visit Victorian wine regions this November appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
The program will start with a field day at Barwon Ridge on Friday 30 November. Image supplied

Winegrowers across the Surf Coast, Moorabool Valley and Bellarine Peninsula will soon have access to a nationally recognised program designed to build healthier, more resilient vineyards.

Following the success of an introductory event held in the Geelong wine region in May 2026, the EcoVineyards program will be formally launching in the region next month.

The program will be open to all winegrowers “interested in improving fruit quality, while building healthier, more productive and resilient vineyards through practical, locally relevant approaches”. The first event is a field day at Barwon Ridge, Barrabool, on Friday 30 November.

EcoVineyards Geelong will offer two free events each year from November 2026 to June 2028, combining practical workshops, vineyard field walks, demonstrations and informal opportunities for winegrowers to exchange knowledge and experiences. The program is delivered by Retallack Viticulture in partnership with Corangamite Catchment Management Authority (CMA), with Bellarine Landcare Group, Geelong Landcare Network, Bellarine Secondary College and Wine Geelong also project partners.

Four EcoGrower demonstration sites will be established across the region, “giving growers the chance to see ecological vineyard management practices in action”. The sites aim to serve as regional learning hubs, showcasing practical regenerative and ecological vineyard management under commercial conditions.

Dr Mary Retallack, managing director of Retallack Viticulture and founder and custodian of EcoVineyards, said the program demonstrates how an understanding of regenerative and ecological processes can help create more resilient and productive vineyards.

“We demonstrate what is possible and share practical approaches that growers can see, understand and adapt to their own vineyards.”

Corangamite CMA Sustainable Agriculture facilitator Karen O’Keefe said she is excited to be expanding the EcoVineyards program to the wider Geelong and Bellarine regions.

“This is the first time Corangamite CMA has delivered a Sustainable Agriculture program specifically focused on viticulture, and it’s a fantastic opportunity to work with local grape growers to build soil health, support biodiversity and strengthen the resilience of vineyards across the region,” O’Keefe said.

“EcoVineyards aligns strongly with our focus on helping landholders adopt practical, sustainable farming practices that support both productive businesses and healthy landscapes.”

Since launching in 2019, EcoVineyards said it has established more than 76 demonstration sites across Australia and delivered more than 100 industry events, “helping winegrowers test and adopt ecological approaches that support resilient vineyard systems”.

title: SIMEI launches new Bevertech exhibition to expand coverage of beverage and liquid food industry
summary:
Italy's wine technology sector continues to dominate globally, accounting for nearly half of the world's wine machinery market, as exhibition SIMEI expands beyond its traditional wine focus with the launch of the new Bevertech exhibition. Bevertech is dedicated to processing and packaging technologies for the wider beverage and liquid food industry. The two events will take place simultaneously at Fiera Milano from 17-20 November 2026, bringing together suppliers and producers from across the wine, beer, spirits, soft drinks, olive oil and liquid food sectors. According to research conducted by MECS (Manufacturing Economic Studies), the combined global market for beverage and liquid food processing and packaging machinery is worth €44.6 billion. Of this total, €16.7 billion relates to sectors traditionally covered by SIMEI, including wine, beer, spirits and olive oil, whilst €27.9 billion comes from the broader beverage and liquid food industries represented by the new Bevertech exhibition.

The post SIMEI launches new Bevertech exhibition to expand coverage of beverage and liquid food industry appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
SIMEI will launch a new Bevertech exhibition at the 2026 event in November. Image supplied

Italy’s wine technology sector continues to dominate globally, accounting for nearly half of the world’s wine machinery market, as exhibition SIMEI expands beyond its traditional wine focus with the launch of the new Bevertech exhibition.

Bevertech is dedicated to processing and packaging technologies for the wider beverage and liquid food industry.

The two events will take place simultaneously at Fiera Milano from 17-20 November 2026, bringing together suppliers and producers from across the wine, beer, spirits, soft drinks, olive oil and liquid food sectors.

According to research conducted by MECS (Manufacturing Economic Studies), the combined global market for beverage and liquid food processing and packaging machinery is worth €44.6 billion. Of this total, €16.7 billion relates to sectors traditionally covered by SIMEI, including wine, beer, spirits and olive oil, whilst €27.9 billion comes from the broader beverage and liquid food industries represented by the new Bevertech exhibition.

SIMEI said this report highlights Italy’s dominant position in the global machinery market, with Italian manufacturers accounting for approximately 21% of the global processing and packaging machinery industry, 47% of the global wine technology sector and 60% of the wine packaging machinery market.

According to the same report, global market for wine processing and packaging machinery was estimated at €2.6 billion in 2025. This includes: €2.03 billion for wine processing equipment, such as crushing, fermentation and filtration systems; and €572.6 million for wine packaging equipment, including bottling, labelling and packaging technologies.

While it says demand for wine processing equipment is expected to remain relatively steady, packaging is forecast to show stronger growth over the coming years.

By 2030, the wine processing machinery market is expected to reach approximately €2.1 billion and the wine packaging sector is forecast to grow to €638.4 million.

Additionally, it explained that Europe accounts for 55% of global demand for wine processing machinery, with the largest national markets being: Italy (€305.2 million), the United States (€263.2 million) and France (€245.4 million).

While growth in Europe is expected to be relatively flat, the report identifies the Asia-Pacific region as one of the most promising growth markets for both wine processing and packaging technologies.

SIMEI said the launch of Bevertech reflects its ambition to expand beyond its traditional wine focus and become a meeting place for the entire beverage and liquid food industry.

Organisers added that the event will connect manufacturers, technology suppliers and producers seeking solutions in automation, efficiency, packaging and process innovation.

title: Beechworth Spring Tasting to return this November
summary:
The Beechworth Wine Region Spring Tasting returns this Saturday 7 November, bringing the region’s winemakers together for “two exceptional tasting sessions at the heart of one of Australia’s most acclaimed wine regions”. Beechworth Vignerons said that for wine lovers, collectors and the wine-curious, the event is “a rare opportunity to experience the breadth of Beechworth Wine Region in one place: meeting the makers, tasting new releases alongside iconic favourites and discovering limited-production wines that can be difficult to find beyond the region”.

The post Beechworth Spring Tasting to return this November appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
The Beechworth Wine Region Spring Tasting returns this Saturday 7 November, bringing the region’s winemakers together for “two exceptional tasting sessions at the heart of one of Australia’s most acclaimed wine regions”.

Beechworth Vignerons said that for wine lovers, collectors and the wine-curious, the event is “a rare opportunity to experience the breadth of Beechworth Wine Region in one place: meeting the makers, tasting new releases alongside iconic favourites and discovering limited-production wines that can be difficult to find beyond the region”.

This year there will be two Saturday sessions with the same line-up of winemakers at each. Session one will take place from 11am to 2pm and session two will be held at 3pm until 6pm. Tickets are $89 per person, per session and the event is 18+ only.

Beechworth Vignerons said the Spring Tasting goes well beyond the traditional cellar door experience.

“Guests can move from producer to producer, talk directly with the people growing the grapes and making the wines, compare varieties and styles, discover new favourites and better understand why this small pocket of the Victorian High Country has earned such an extraordinary reputation for wine,” the organisation explained.

The region will also be hosting more events across the weekend, including a Rare Wines Dinner, Chardonnay Masterclass and Anything But Chardonnay Masterclass.

Details for the masterclasses and dinner are as follows:

Rare Wines Dinner

  • Saturday 7 November
  • 7:00pm Ford Street Enoteca, Beechworth
  • $195 per person
  • Seats are strictly limited and are already selling quickly

Chardonnay Masterclass

  • Explore the variety that helped put Beechworth on the world wine map
  • Sunday 8 November
  • 11:00am – 12:30pm Tanswell’s Commercial Hotel
  • $120 per person

Anything But Chardonnay Masterclass

  • Look beyond the region’s famous Chardonnay and explore the diversity of Beechworth through alternative varieties and regional favourites
  • Sunday 8 November
  • 2:00pm – 3:30pm Tanswell’s Commercial Hotel
  • $120 per person

Tickets and more information are available here.

title: The sparkle in a bust
summary:
Felicity Edwards, director at global consulting firm AlixPartners in Sydney, examines Australia’s wine industry in crisis, but argues one category is bucking the trend. Red production collapsed by 29%, and exports declined to their lowest level since 2004. As set out in From Boom to Surplus, this is a structural shift that will continue amid oversupply, declining per-capita wine consumption in developed markets, and premiumisation pressures that have hollowed out the middle market, Edwards writes.

The post The sparkle in a bust appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
Why Australian sparkling is where smart wine money goes

Felicity Edwards, director at global consulting firm AlixPartners in Sydney, examines Australia’s wine industry in crisis, but argues one category is bucking the trend. Now, she says, it needs ‘capital and punch’.

This year’s National Vintage Report put the 2026 crush at just 1.27 million tonnes, down 19 per cent year-on-year, the smallest harvest this century. Red production collapsed by 29%, and exports declined to their lowest level since 2004. As set out in From Boom to Surplus, this is a structural shift that will continue amid oversupply, declining per-capita wine consumption in developed markets, and premiumisation pressures that have hollowed out the middle market.

Within this crisis sits an outlier. One category has held its ground globally while every other style has fallen. Australia is building world-class credentials in this space – but not fast enough or far enough.

That category is sparkling wine.

Where sparkle still grows

Over the past two decades, sparkling wine has grown faster than any other category. As of 2023, sparkling wine accounted for 20% of global wine sales by value, despite representing only 7% of global wine production.

While consumption has slowed, the category has reached US$55B. The nuance is the real story: growth has moved to both ends of the category.

  • The accessible end is growing: sparkling is now a wine for all occasions (Prosecco DOC increased by 1.1% to 667 million bottles and Crémant has grown +44% over the past five years, with an average retail price of around AU$11)
  • The premium end is expanding (Prosecco DOCG grew 8% to 98 million bottles and Cava’s ultra-premium Paraje Calificado nearly doubled, even as Cava overall fell 13%)
  • The classic centre is contracting (Champagne has shrunk every year since its 2022 peak, down another 2% in 2025 to 266 million bottles, with revenue falling 12%)

In addition, no/low alcohol wine has grown by 8% per annum over the past decade. With sparkling wines making up half of the category, reaching around 160 million bottles, this is the fastest growing segment in sparkling.

Australia’s competitive advantage

Sparkling wine thrives in cool climates. High acidity, low alcohol potential, and tension between fruit and minerality create complex and age-worthy sparkling that can compete with Champagne.

Because of this, Australia already produces critically acclaimed sparkling wines at AU$30-50 that deliver parity on quality (and, in some cases, superiority) against Champagne and the rising English sparkling category, which can be priced 2-3x higher:

House of Arras (Tasmania): Chairman’s Trophy at the 2024 Champagne & Sparkling Wine World Championships – the first ever for Australia

Ed Carr, House of Arras Chief Winemaker: IWC Sparkling Winemaker of the Year – only the second non-Champenois winemaker in 40 years – now twice over (2024 and 2026)

Domestic recognition runs deeper still, with Deviation Road (Adelaide Hills), Stefano Lubiana (Tasmania), and Chandon (Yarra Valley) all taking top domestic honours.

Quality is proven. Execution, supply reliability and brand differentiation will determine the winners.

The investment case

Sparkling wine presents a rare convergence for capital deployment:

  • Category resilience: the wine style holding its ground in a contracting wine market
  • Proven quality parity: awards remove the ‘but is it really as good?’ objection
  • Price advantage: Australian sparkling competes on price where Champagne’s cost base makes it uneconomic to follow
  • Multiple operating models: Scale (Chandon, Jansz) plays alongside boutique/allocation models (House of Arras, Deviation Road)
  • Demonstrated value premium: Tasmania earns 6.5% of national wine value from 1.2% of production, a five-fold premium the market is already paying

These insights and numbers make the investment case compelling, but capital is only half the puzzle.

The three challenges

  1. Production and supply chain

Many Australian cool-climate producers already grow the grapes needed for sparkling. Here, the opportunity lies in converting production methodology and holding periods rather than replanting. But conversion is capital-hungry: traditional-method sparkling requires long ageing. Deviation Road’s Beltana is aged for seven years before release.

One route shortens the cycle: low/no alcohol sparkling is the fastest growing segment and de-alcholised wine does not carry the multi-year ageing burden, providing a faster return on the same fruit

Further, award-winning Australian sparkling wines are already supply-constrained. Scaling without destroying scarcity that justifies premium pricing is a fine balance. Patient capital solves this through investing in:

  • Expanding vineyard acreage in cool regions
  • Production equipment for méthode traditionnelle
  • Working capital infrastructure to manage multi-year ageing cycles
  • De-alcoholisation capability as a shorter-cycle revenue stream
  • Allocation/club models that sustain scarcity pricing while improving accessibility

Scarcity supports premium pricing and allocation models, but capital is tied up for 3-10 years before ROI, and long ageing can squeeze margin rather than build it.

 

  1. Market accessibility and distribution

Tasmania exports just 6% of what its crush. The region winning international sparkling trophies sells almost all of it at home.

That is the gap. Award-winning Australian sparkling wines are difficult to find outside Australia despite global accolades. English sparkling solved this through aggressive supermarket and on-trade placement.

High-growth markets with low entrenched Australian wine identity provide a blank canvas for brand-building. What is needed is a distribution infrastructure.

Investment opportunity:

  • Distributor partnerships in the UK, US, and Asia-Pacific
  • On-trade education programmes (restaurants, bars, hotels)
  • Sommelier tasting tours to build trade awareness

Strategic market entry requires sustained presence and education, along with a quality product.

 

  1. Brand recognition and credibility

Australian wine identity is still synonymous with cheap bulk red in key export markets. Awards prove quality but don’t automatically convert to market perception or premium positioning. English sparkling shifted perception with a positioning claim (‘Champagne terroir in the UK’) and the evidence to back it (Chapel Down took 60% in a blind tasting against Moët).

Australia must claim its own positioning: cool-climate Southern Hemisphere sparkling, priced accessibly with the trophy shelf to prove it.

Investment unlocks:

  • Competition participation (CSWWC, IWC, Decanter) to build award credentials
  • Critic and influencer engagement to amplify award wins
  • Targeted storytelling positioning terroir and price advantage

English sparkling’s playbook is proven: execution matters. Australian producers need the marketing budget to tell that story.

The window is open

England proved the global market will embrace ‘Champagne alternatives’ when quality is demonstrable and price justified. Australia has the same assets and better economics: quality, climate advantage, lower price points and award credentials. What it lacks is capital, distribution, and marketing to translate regional excellence into a global position.

While the global wine industry is contracting, sparkling is the one category holding its ground, and within it, the money is moving to the ends: accessible and genuinely premium. Australia can occupy both. It is already doing so at home.

That bright spark in the global wine crisis? It is Australian.

Sources: Wine Australia, IWSR, Euromonitor, ProWein

title: Tasmanian wine community reflects on a year of awards and achievements
summary:
On Tuesday 20 October, the Tasmanian wine community celebrated its achievements at the 2026 Tassie Wine Stars event. Joe Chromy AO was inducted as a new Wine Tasmania Life Member “in recognition of his significant and long-term contribution to the Tasmanian wine sector”. Wine Tasmania said his incredible life story is well-known and celebrated in the Tassie wine community, including his development of Rochecombe, Heemskerk, Jansz, Tamar Ridge and Josef Chromy Wines. Terry Bennett of Home Hill Wines was announced as the 2026 Wine Tasmania Legend “for his significant and continuing contribution to Tasmanian wine, particularly Pinot Noir viticulture and as reflected in Home Hill being one of the island’s most awarded wine producers”.

The post Tasmanian wine community reflects on a year of awards and achievements appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
On Tuesday 20 October, the Tasmanian wine community celebrated its achievements at the 2026 Tassie Wine Stars event.

Joe Chromy AO was inducted as a new Wine Tasmania Life Member “in recognition of his significant and long-term contribution to the Tasmanian wine sector”.

Wine Tasmania said his incredible life story is well-known and celebrated in the Tassie wine community, including his development of Rochecombe, Heemskerk, Jansz, Tamar Ridge and Josef Chromy Wines.

Terry Bennett of Home Hill Wines was announced as the 2026 Wine Tasmania Legend “for his significant and continuing contribution to Tasmanian wine, particularly Pinot Noir viticulture and as reflected in Home Hill being one of the island’s most awarded wine producers”.

A wide range of achievements during the year were celebrated, including wine show trophies to Dalrymple Vineyards, Pooley Wines, Bream Creek Vineyard, Josef Chromy Wines, Decades, Freycinet Vineyard and House of Arras, with the latter’s winemaker, Ed Carr, being named Sparkling Winemaker of the Year at the 2026 International Wine Challenge for the second time as the only non-European to receive this award.

Wine Tasmania CEO Sheralee Davies reflected on a significant year for Tasmanian wine and its talented wine producers.

“It’s been another brilliant year for Tasmania’s wine community, reflected in numerous awards and achievements. We’ve also seen continued strong global recognition of Tassie’s wines, including sold-out wine trade events in Singapore, Seoul, Sydney and Melbourne during the year.

“The Tassie Wine Stars event celebrates both recent successes and the substantial contribution of the many people who have positively impacted our wine sector. We’re delighted to induct Joe Chromy AO as a new Wine Tasmania Life Member and to award Terry Bennett the Wine Tasmania Legend Award in 2026.”

The 2026 Tasmanian Wine Sector Environmental Sustainability Report was also released at the event and the 2026 sustainability awards announced.

Pooley Wines in the Coal River Valley was announced as the 2026 VinØ (‘vin zero’) Program Champion and Westella Vineyard in the Tamar Valley was awarded the 2026 VinØ Program’s Most Improved Producer. The VinØ Program was initiated in 2015, “providing a tailored best practice management program to help the island’s growers and makers measure, improve and report on their sustainability”.

Wine Tasmania’s 20th AGM was held earlier in the day, with two new directors appointed — Fran Austin (Delamere Vineyards) and Kathryn Bevan (Handpicked Wines), with Tim Lyne (Spring Vale Wines) reappointed for another term.

Retiring directors Nick Haddow (Haddow & Dineen Wines) and Alicia Peardon (Ghost Rock Wines), who served eight and three years respectively, were thanked for their board service.

The 2026 Tasmanian Wine Sustainability Report is available here.

title: Sparkling Spring weekend back on at Sidewood with exclusive product launch
summary:
Sidewood Estate is celebrating spring in the Adelaide Hills with its annual Sparkling Spring weekend on 24 and 25 October, bringing together wine, food, live music and outdoor experiences at its Hahndorf estate. Saturday’s event is the Sparkling Spring Party, an 18+ celebration running from 11:30am to 5pm. Guests will be given a complimentary glass of Sidewood sparkling wine on arrival, festival-style food by executive chef Nick Filsell, live DJ sets from Harvey Robbins, a glitter bar and lawn games. At the celebration, Sidewood will officially launch its newest product Suncello. The winery described Suncello as bright and refreshing, explaining that it has been created to enjoy chilled and can be used as the base of a simple spritz. 250 dozen have been produced for this first release, with guests attending Saturday’s event among the first to try the new addition to Sidewood’s portfolio

content:
The event will run across Saturday and Sunday, with different attractions on each day. Image supplied

Sidewood Estate is celebrating spring in the Adelaide Hills with its annual Sparkling Spring weekend on 24 and 25 October, bringing together wine, food, live music and outdoor experiences at its Hahndorf estate.

Saturday’s event is the Sparkling Spring Party, an 18+ celebration running from 11:30am to 5pm. Guests will be given a complimentary glass of Sidewood sparkling wine on arrival, festival-style food by executive chef Nick Filsell, live DJ sets from Harvey Robbins, a glitter bar and lawn games.

At the celebration, Sidewood will officially launch its newest product Suncello. The winery described Suncello as bright and refreshing, explaining that it has been created to enjoy chilled and can be used as the base of a simple spritz. 250 dozen have been produced for this first release, with guests attending Saturday’s event among the first to try the new addition to Sidewood’s portfolio.

On Sunday, Sidewood will open its gardens for a free-entry Family Fun Day from 11:30am to 5pm with live music, face painting, glitter, bubbles, lawn games and ice cream. Food by Chef Nick and Sidewood wines will be available to purchase throughout the afternoon.

Tickets to Saturday’s 18+ event are $35 and available here.

content:
South Australian wines will continue to be showcased at La Cité du Vin, a prestigious wine museum in France, following a new two-year deal signed by the state government.

Attracting more than 3.5 million visitors from across the world since it was established a decade ago, La Cité du Vin “delivers immersive showcases of the world’s best wines”.

The new Memorandum of Understanding between the SA government and the wine museum in Bordeaux was signed on the eve of the Great Wine Capitals Global Network’s International Annual Conference, which is currently underway in Hawke’s Bay, New Zealand.

Through this renewed partnership, South Australian winemakers will showcase their wines through tastings in the museum’s Belvedere Room, “against a 360-degree panoramic backdrop of Bordeaux”.

South Australian wine producers will also host special events and deliver tasting masterclasses at the museum.

Clare Scriven MLC, Minister for Primary Industries and Regional Development, said the deal secures SA’s place in the world’s most prestigious wine museum.

“South Australia is home to an extraordinary wine industry, with iconic producers with global reputations and emerging winemakers who are working hard to make their mark around the world.

“Partnerships like this help South Australia share its story with new audiences, build new connections between local producers and international consumers, and support the long-term growth of our wine and tourism industries,” Minister Scriven said.

Florence Maffrand, head of wine partnerships & international patronage at La Cite du Vin, said they are delighted to continue the partnership.

“Since 2016, the mission of the Foundation for wine culture and civilisations has been to share the universal heritage of wine with visitors to La Cité du Vin. We want to spark curiosity, encourage discovery and, above all, make visitors want to go further, to continue this journey elsewhere.

“Our wine partners are at the heart of what we offer; they are truly indispensable. Wines are essential to creating experiences with our audiences: they allow us to deepen our understanding of wine cultures around the world,” Maffrand said.

Minister for Tourism Emily Bourke added that the venue provides incredible exposure for SA wineries, with nearly 400,000 people visiting the museum last year.

“Initiatives like this and South Australia’s recent success in the Michelin Guide, with 77 restaurants now featured in the global culinary bible, reinforces our state’s growing reputation as a must-visit destination for world-class wine and food.”

The state has been showcasing its wine at the institution since 2017, with forty SA wine producers having been showcased at La Cité du Vin to date.

Jo Collins, Great Wine Capitals Global Network president, said the partnership renewal is an important investment in the global recognition of SA’s wine industry and the people behind it.

“Through our collaboration with the museum, we can showcase our exceptional wine producers to international audiences, share the stories behind our world-class wine regions and continue to strengthen Adelaide’s profile as a globally competitive wine and tourism destination.

“This partnership creates valuable opportunities to celebrate South Australia’s wine excellence on the world stage, and we look forward to continuing our work with the museum to raise the profile of our wine producers and regions internationally.”

The SA government shared that the collaboration has also enabled a portrait of Munda Wines owner and founder Pauly Vandenbergh to be featured at La Cité du Vin’s international photography exhibition, which is currently open to the public until the end of the year.

South Australia produces 80 per cent of Australia’s premium wine and 50 per cent of all bottled wine. The sector supports more than 90,000 jobs, includes almost 700 wineries and more than 70,000 hectares of vines.
